genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure works as a repairer of technical objects
she starts with the energy cells
she can tell in advance which cells will run too hot
she is also drawn to very small drive motors
she opens sealed housings without harming the gasket
her workroom is cramped and poorly lit
she keeps her screws sorted by size
she greets and informs curious passers-by
she refuses to discard an object she has not examined
she machines the parts she cannot find
text: Walk past her door and you would never guess her occupation in the back room. She fixes broken gear for a living, and among everything reaching her bench, batteries come first. She opens them, coaxes a charge back into them, and knows which ones will overheat before ever connecting them. Tiny motors hold her next, the sort demanding fine pliers to release a bent shaft. Then come the housings, above all the sealed ones you have to crack open without ruining the gasket. Her workroom is one dim space: a bench, a swing-arm lamp, drawers of screws sorted by size. She likes explaining the trade to anyone curious enough to push the door open, and she will not throw out a device she has not opened yet. When a part cannot be had, she cuts it herself, filing a blank of metal all evening long if that is what the job takes.

units: the maker promised a week of use with no charging
the unboxing gives a flattering first impression
the device is described as very light
the display stays readable under strong light
the machine makes no noise during demanding work
after long use the shell warms up near the hinge
battery life drops once the radio link is switched on
a software fix has not removed the typing lag
the reviewer finds the price too high for what is offered
text: A week away from an outlet with nothing to plug into: that was the maker's claim for this small handheld reader. Unpacked, the promise looks believable: a matte shell, a hinge that clicks firmly under the thumb, a body almost weightless in the hand. The first sessions do nothing to spoil that. The screen stays readable in hard sun, and the thing never makes a sound, not even while it grinds through a heavy file. A week on, the mood cools. The shell grows warm near the hinge, and the battery life on the box melts away the moment the wireless link goes on. An update has since gone out and fixed part of that, yet the keys still lag behind the fingers. Call it a pleasant machine, roughly finished, and asking far more of the wallet than it hands back. The next one may be worth the wait.

units: the writer is writing from his workroom
an old sound receiver sits beside him
the reader had predicted that the device was beyond saving
a damaged electrical wire cut the sound at the slightest knock
the writer mended the link by soldering it again
damp had made the wooden case swell
the top no longer fitted into its housing
sanding restored the sliding of the lid
the device now keeps the writer company in the evenings
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see the result
text: I am writing to you from the workroom, the window open onto the yard, the old radio beside me on the bench. You told me it would never work again, and you were nearly right: a wire had frayed inside it, so the sound dropped out whenever anyone brushed the table. I stripped the cable back, soldered the two strands together again, and the crackle went away all at once. Damp had worked its way into the case as well. The wood swelled, the lid no longer dropped into its groove, so I sanded it patiently until it slid as before. Now the voices fill the room once night falls, and I drift off with them still going, never touching the volume. You see, it took almost nothing at all in the end. Come by whenever you can and hear for yourself how it sings, now that it breathes freely again.

units: the readings of a heat sensor become inaccurate
the sensing element is usually not to blame
a deposit of particles on the wall disturbs the flow of heat
replacing the whole unit is not necessary
cleaning followed by adjustment on two fixed marks is enough
checking means comparing the values with those of a control instrument
a steady offset can be taken up by the software
an erratic swing reveals a loss of sealing in the housing
the gasket must be renewed before readings start again
text: What is going on when a heat sensor stops giving readings you can trust? The probe itself is seldom to blame. Dust settles on the membrane and gets in the way of the heat exchange, and the drift begins right there. Does the whole unit need swapping out? Hardly ever. Clean the membrane, then set the instrument against two steady reference marks, and the trouble usually ends. How can you tell the work took? Leave the sensor beside a known-good instrument for a good stretch and compare what each one gives. A constant offset points to a leftover shift, and the software can take care of that. And when the gap wanders with no pattern behind it? The housing has most likely lost its seal, letting damp reach the contacts. Fit a fresh gasket before you begin another round of readings.

units: a technical manager asks a skilled worker about the choice of a machine
two devices are weighed against each other
the older device runs without any electrical supply
it is started by a foot control
the newer device is markedly faster
the newer device stops by itself when something jams
the newer device calls for regular upkeep
the older one is mended with basic tools
the two speakers decide to keep both machines
a second look at the choice is planned after a season of use
text: The engineer asked the technician which of the two systems he would rather have standing on the workshop floor. He spoke up for the older one: purely mechanical, worked by a pedal under the foot, and tied to no electrical supply at all. She pushed back. The newer machine runs far quicker, she said, and it halts on its own the instant a part jams. He granted her that much, then reminded her what the newer one wants in return, steady upkeep week after week, while the old one can be put right with a wrench and some patience. Her proposal was to keep both machines and to bring the powered model in only for the long runs. He agreed, but on one condition: the crew must learn to handle the old one properly first. They settled on taking up the question again once a full season of work has gone by.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping sounds meant finding a way to write them down
the first method cut a groove with a vibrating point
this method made it possible to bring a voice back later
the second method rested on magnetizing a ribbon coated with grains
magnetizing allowed the content to be wiped and written again
the third method turned the signal into a run of separate values
each method changed practices as much as devices
recordings became in turn portable, copyable without loss, then freed from any object
this change is presented as a series of trade-offs between quality, sturdiness and ease of copying
text: Before sound could be carried anywhere, someone had to work out how to hold it still. The first answer was mechanical. A needle tied to a membrane cut a groove into soft material, so that a voice could be carved down and brought back long afterward. The second answer was magnetic. A ribbon coated in fine grains held the pull of a field, which meant a recording could be wiped and written over. The third answer counted instead: the smooth signal was chopped into a string of separate values, stored, and put back together on playback. Every one of these steps reshaped what people did as much as what they owned. Recordings turned portable, then copyable with nothing lost, then loose from any object at all. Read from end to end, the story amounts to a run of bargains struck among quality, sturdiness and ease of copying.

units: sending a message sets off its cutting into very short pieces
each piece carries a mark showing the address it is bound for
the pieces first travel through the air to the nearest relay
walls and structures are not enough to stop that relay from hearing them
the pieces then run on through buried or underwater cables
their route changes at every node according to congestion
the receiving device puts the pieces back in the right order
the whole trip takes an extremely short time
a lost piece is asked for again automatically without the user noticing
text: Consider what becomes of your message the second you tap send. Your handset chops it into tiny pieces and pins a label on every one of them, saying where it has to end up. Off they go through the air to the nearest tower, which manages to hear your handset through however many walls happen to stand in the way. From there they run along cables, mostly buried beneath streets or laid across the seabed, and at every junction they pick a fresh route depending on how crowded the last one is. They come down at the far end, where the receiving handset sorts them back into order and rebuilds the sentence you wrote. The whole trip is over faster than a blink, however far it had to go. And if a piece goes astray on the way, your handset quietly asks for it again, and you never notice a thing.

units: the night crew took no notice of a stopped fan in a technical cabinet
the coolness of the room discouraged any immediate action
the heat sensor had been shifted the day before because of wiring work
it was reading the temperature of a nearby corridor instead of the trapped hot air
no alarm went off despite the building heat
two storage units failed toward the end of the night
the incident cut off mail service for a very large public
the inquiry blames the failure on the unrecorded shifting of the sensor
a written procedure now covers any change in the position of a sensor
text: The whole thing started with a detail that the night crew shrugged off at first: the fan on one of the computer cabinets had gone quiet. The room itself felt cool, so nobody saw any reason to go and look into it before morning. But the heat probe had been shifted the day before to make room for cabling work, and it was now reading the air of the corridor next door instead of the stale air trapped behind the machines. So the heat built up behind them and no alarm ever sounded. Toward dawn two of the drives gave out, and mail service went down for many thousands of users. The internal report put the failure not on the hardware but on a probe that had been moved without anyone writing the move down anywhere. Ever since, shifting a sensor anywhere calls for a written note and a check the following day.

units: a hand-cranked torch stops working when its generator seizes
it is advised to lay the object on a light-colored cloth
this precaution keeps the screws from being lost
the four fasteners in the base come out before the two half-shells are parted
the parting must be gentle so as to spare the catches
the coil of wire turns out to be fouled with a greasy deposit
cleaning is done dry before the shaft bearing is oiled
a lingering squeak comes from the return spring, which has to be tightened
putting it back together means not driving the screws home at once
the light comes back little by little after long cranking
text: A hand-cranked flashlight usually ends up dead at the back of a drawer, the reason nearly always being a seized dynamo. Here is how to bring it back to life. Lay it on a pale cloth first, so that no screw can vanish against the surface. Take out the four screws in the base, then ease the two shells apart slowly, without straining the catches. Inside sits a gray coil furred with greasy dust matting the windings together. Brush it clean while it is dry, work the shaft free, and put one drop of light oil on the bearing. If the crank squeaks even then, the return spring is the culprit: unhook it and pull it back to tension. Close the shells, start the screws without driving them home, and turn the crank for a good long while. The beam will come back, faint at first, then full and steady.

units: the managers of a water supply have weighed two monitoring systems
the two systems are fitted to comparable pipes
the first uses pressure sensors wired to the mains supply
these sensors talk over a shielded wired link
the first gives very frequent readings and flags a water loss quickly
the second rests on standalone sensors closed inside a watertight case
the second sends its data over a radio link that draws little power
the second offers less precision but spares any digging work
the study recommends the wired one on sensitive stretches and the standalone one on distant branches
both systems depend on a water-flow model kept up to date by operators
text: The people running a water network have just weighed two monitoring setups fitted to twin mains. The first works from pressure sensors drawing power from the grid, wired back to a central controller over shielded cable. It reports at very short intervals and catches a leak long before the next round of readings. The second uses standalone probes sealed inside a watertight case, sending what they measure over a radio link that sips power. Its resolution is coarser, but putting it in place calls for no trench at all. The report lands on a split answer: keep the wired build on the stretches that matter most, where a leak costs dearly, and hand the far-flung branches to the standalone probes. Both share one weakness, a reliance on a water-flow model that someone has to update by hand.
